messages.subject: Error in multi-species occupancy prediction
parts:
Hi,

I want to use prediction function of multi-species occupancy. So I run the code exactly as what the CamtrapR example showed:

predictions_psi <- predict(object    = model1_jags,
                           mcmc.list = out_ahm_jags,
                           x         = habitat,
                           type      = "psi",
                           draws     = 1000)

However, I got the error like:

Error in out_intercept[, i, ] <- posterior_matrix[, colnames(posterior_matrix) %in%  :
  replacement has length zero 

I am sure that I have added all the raster of occupancy covariates which I added in my previous model.

Any help on what this error means or how to slove this error is greatly appreciated. 
Thanks in advance!

Peiyun

messages.author: 0b86ca0cb4b615b0
messages.subject: Re: [camtrapR] Re: Error in multi-species occupancy prediction
parts:
Hi,
the "error: cannot allocate vector of size 1.7 Gb" is an out-of-memory error, as you mentioned. Large predictions (especially spatial) with many posterior draws and many species can be extremely memory intensive. There are intermediate objects of dimension: n(sites) x n(species) x n(draws), so we quickly get billions of cells and R objects several Gb large. Fewer posterior draws or smaller prediction raster can help if memory is limited.

The other error: "only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts" means that R is trying to use negative and positive indices, e.g. x[-1:1], which is not expected behaviour. That is likely a problem related to one of your covariates. Do you have factor covariates in the prediction raster stack? If yes, are they formatted correctly (values are integer numbers indicating the factor level of a cell)? Or do you possibly have negative values (e.g. due to scale()) in the factor covariate of the prediction raster?
Feel free to share the summary() of the raster stack if you're uncertain.

Last point, what exactly do you mean by true occupancy value? Occupancy probability or occupancy status (1/0). Occupancy probability can also be calculated with predict(). Simply provide a data frame with the covariate values at the stations to the function instead of a covariate raster. But be aware that the occupancy probabilities are theoretical, so even with confirmed occupancy at a station (occupancy status = 1) the probability will be <1.

Another possibility, you can return the z matrix (occupancy status for each station & species) from the model. It is not returned by default, but you can include it in the monitored model parameters:
 
mod.jags <- communityModel(...)
mod.jags@params <- c(mod.jags@params, "z")  # monitor parameter z
fit(...)

Thank you,
Jürgen

messages.subject: Re: [camtrapR] Re: Error in multi-species occupancy prediction
parts:
Hi,
what I called fit.jags above is called out_ahm_jags in your example. It is the mcmc.list object that is created by the fit() function.

This line:
DT::datatable(round(summary(out_ahm_jags)$statistics, 3))
returns summary statistics of the model parameters (rounded) in a nicely formatted html table (hence z is not binary, because it is a summary of 0s and 1s).

So in your case out_ahm_jags[, "z"] should give the raw z output.

And yes, you get z (and all other parameters) from 3 chains. For summary statistics the estimates of the 3 chains are combined, which is why it is important to check convergence (to ensure the chains are sampling the same distribution).

If you want to know exactly how z is calculated please see the model code. It is
z[i,j] ~ dbern(psi[i, j])
where i is the species index and j the station index. So for each species and station, z (occupancy status) is a random Bernoulli trial with the respective occupancy probability.

Species richness in the predictions is based on this z matrix. Richness is simply the sum over all species at a given location (usually raster cell). So unlike the quote you shared (which used oberserved species richness + estimated richness of unobserved species), the richness calculations in predict() uses only the z matrix and ignores observed richness. This is because when predicting on a raster we don't have observed richness information for most cells. 

The quote refers to richness predictions at sampling locations only (where observed richness is known), whereas predict(..., type = "richness") treats all locations as unsampled (even if you use the function for estimating richness at camera trap stations only).
While I agree it is a good suggestion to include observed richness in richness predictions at camera trap stations, I am afraid won't have time to implement it anytime soon. One can probably find a hacky way to implement it by:

1) running predict() separately for each station
2) using the speciesSubset argument to predict only to unobserved species (at each station)
3) summing up observed richness and richness of unobserved species

Best regards,
Jürgen

On Thursday, 1 December 2022 at 07:26:05 UTC+8 Juergen Niedballa wrote:
Hi,
the "error: cannot allocate vector of size 1.7 Gb" is an out-of-memory error, as you mentioned. Large predictions (especially spatial) with many posterior draws and many species can be extremely memory intensive. There are intermediate objects of dimension: n(sites) x n(species) x n(draws), so we quickly get billions of cells and R objects several Gb large. Fewer posterior draws or smaller prediction raster can help if memory is limited.

The other error: "only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts" means that R is trying to use negative and positive indices, e.g. x[-1:1], which is not expected behaviour. That is likely a problem related to one of your covariates. Do you have factor covariates in the prediction raster stack? If yes, are they formatted correctly (values are integer numbers indicating the factor level of a cell)? Or do you possibly have negative values (e.g. due to scale()) in the factor covariate of the prediction raster?
Feel free to share the summary() of the raster stack if you're uncertain.

Last point, what exactly do you mean by true occupancy value? Occupancy probability or occupancy status (1/0). Occupancy probability can also be calculated with predict(). Simply provide a data frame with the covariate values at the stations to the function instead of a covariate raster. But be aware that the occupancy probabilities are theoretical, so even with confirmed occupancy at a station (occupancy status = 1) the probability will be <1.

Another possibility, you can return the z matrix (occupancy status for each station & species) from the model. It is not returned by default, but you can include it in the monitored model parameters:
 
mod.jags <- communityModel(...)
mod.jags@params <- c(mod.jags@params, "z")  # monitor parameter z
fit(...)

Thank you,
Jürgen

messages.subject: Re: [camtrapR] Re: Error in multi-species occupancy prediction
parts:
Richness estimations for species subsets are implemented already in the predict() function. Use argument speciesSubset to select the species and set type = "richness".
Then you don't need to deal with the z matrices at all (which is currently derived from psi anyways and does not use the observed occupancy status).

Also, correction from my earlier reply. The z parameters are indexed by species and station, so you can obtain them via e.g.
out_ahm_jags[, "z[1,2]"]   #  1st species, 2nd station

That also means that creating the z matrix from the model estimates is a little more involved. Let me know if you need more information about how to recreate the z matrices.
Best,
J

messages.subject: Re: [camtrapR] Re: Error in multi-species occupancy prediction
parts:
The latest version on Github now gives species richness estimates for each station directly in the model output (as a monitored parameter in the model). The parameter is called "Nspecies_stations" and is only returned in JAGS models.

It sums up the z matrix in the model in which a species with observed presence at a given station will always count as 1, and unobserved species may or may not be 1 (based on their occupancy probability). That is basically what the formula you shared above does.

That is in contrast to the predict() method mentioned before which used beta parameters and covariate values to predict psi and then z, and does not take into account observed detections.

On Thursday, 12 January 2023 at 13:41:24 UTC+8 Juergen Niedballa wrote:
Hi,
what I called fit.jags above is called out_ahm_jags in your example. It is the mcmc.list object that is created by the fit() function.

This line:
DT::datatable(round(summary(out_ahm_jags)$statistics, 3))
returns summary statistics of the model parameters (rounded) in a nicely formatted html table (hence z is not binary, because it is a summary of 0s and 1s).

So in your case out_ahm_jags[, "z"] should give the raw z output.

And yes, you get z (and all other parameters) from 3 chains. For summary statistics the estimates of the 3 chains are combined, which is why it is important to check convergence (to ensure the chains are sampling the same distribution).

If you want to know exactly how z is calculated please see the model code. It is
z[i,j] ~ dbern(psi[i, j])
where i is the species index and j the station index. So for each species and station, z (occupancy status) is a random Bernoulli trial with the respective occupancy probability.

Species richness in the predictions is based on this z matrix. Richness is simply the sum over all species at a given location (usually raster cell). So unlike the quote you shared (which used oberserved species richness + estimated richness of unobserved species), the richness calculations in predict() uses only the z matrix and ignores observed richness. This is because when predicting on a raster we don't have observed richness information for most cells. 

The quote refers to richness predictions at sampling locations only (where observed richness is known), whereas predict(..., type = "richness") treats all locations as unsampled (even if you use the function for estimating richness at camera trap stations only).
While I agree it is a good suggestion to include observed richness in richness predictions at camera trap stations, I am afraid won't have time to implement it anytime soon. One can probably find a hacky way to implement it by:

1) running predict() separately for each station
2) using the speciesSubset argument to predict only to unobserved species (at each station)
3) summing up observed richness and richness of unobserved species

Best regards,
Jürgen

On Thursday, 1 December 2022 at 07:26:05 UTC+8 Juergen Niedballa wrote:
Hi,
the "error: cannot allocate vector of size 1.7 Gb" is an out-of-memory error, as you mentioned. Large predictions (especially spatial) with many posterior draws and many species can be extremely memory intensive. There are intermediate objects of dimension: n(sites) x n(species) x n(draws), so we quickly get billions of cells and R objects several Gb large. Fewer posterior draws or smaller prediction raster can help if memory is limited.

The other error: "only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts" means that R is trying to use negative and positive indices, e.g. x[-1:1], which is not expected behaviour. That is likely a problem related to one of your covariates. Do you have factor covariates in the prediction raster stack? If yes, are they formatted correctly (values are integer numbers indicating the factor level of a cell)? Or do you possibly have negative values (e.g. due to scale()) in the factor covariate of the prediction raster?
Feel free to share the summary() of the raster stack if you're uncertain.

Last point, what exactly do you mean by true occupancy value? Occupancy probability or occupancy status (1/0). Occupancy probability can also be calculated with predict(). Simply provide a data frame with the covariate values at the stations to the function instead of a covariate raster. But be aware that the occupancy probabilities are theoretical, so even with confirmed occupancy at a station (occupancy status = 1) the probability will be <1.

Another possibility, you can return the z matrix (occupancy status for each station & species) from the model. It is not returned by default, but you can include it in the monitored model parameters:
 
mod.jags <- communityModel(...)
mod.jags@params <- c(mod.jags@params, "z")  # monitor parameter z
fit(...)

Thank you,
Jürgen
